A **mixed model**, **mixed-effects model** or **mixed error-component model** is a statistical model containing both fixed effects and random effects. Linear mixed models (LMMs) are statistical models that incorporate fixed and random effects to accurately represent non-independent data structures. A key component of the mixed model is the incorporation of random effects with the fixed effect. Subsequently, mixed modeling has become a major area of statistical research, including work on computation of maximum likelihood estimates, non-linear mixed effects models, missing data in mixed effects models, and Bayesian estimation of mixed effects models. results.title: Fixed or random? On the reliability of mixed-effects models for a small number of levels in grouping variables
results.content: Fixed- and mixed-effects models fit to simulated data with random intercept (a,b) and random intercept and slope (c,d) for each mountain in the example from H2 Box 1. To understand how the number of levels affected the estimation of the standard deviation of the random effect in mixed-effects models, we recorded and compared standard deviation estimates for random intercepts and slopes from the correctly specified mixed-effects model in scenario B (Table 1, Eq. 10). Type I error rates, power, and coverage for linear fixed and mixed effect models (A) and generalized linear fixed and mixed-effects models (B), fitted to simulated data with 2-8 mountains (random intercept for each mountain - Scenario A) and 50 observations per mountain. Type I error rates, power, and coverage for linear (mixed effect) models (A) and generalized linear (mixed-effects) models (B), fitted to simulated data with 2-8 mountains for scenario B (random intercept and random slope for each mountain range). In comparison, the fixed effect model had similar type I error rates for data that presented singular and non-singular fits in mixed-effects models, both increasing towards the nominal value with increasing number of groups (Fig. 4C). Here, we showed with simulations that mixed-effects models with small number of levels in the grouping variable are more robust than previously assumed (Fig. 3) and that the decision between fixed and random effect matters most when the data-generating processes also included a varying slope for each group (Fig. 2). The standard deviation estimates of the random effects of a correctly fitted model (no-singular fit) were around the correct value, showing that mixed-effects models were able to correctly estimate the random effect variance for a small number of groups (McNeish 2017), although with a higher uncertainty (Fig. 3B). Coming back to our original question, we found no harsh threshold for the minimum number of levels in a grouping variable necessary to model it as a random effect (Fig. 2), but rather found that a singular fit in the mixed-effects model indicates switching to the fixed-effects model is beneficial (more conservative type I error rates, Fig. 2).
